name: wait_for_workstream
description: Block until one or all named child workstreams reach a terminal state. Prefer this over busy-polling inspect_workstream after a fan-out: the tool absorbs the wait, so you get one call + one result regardless of duration. Returns `{results: {ws_id: {state, tokens, updated, name, message, truncated}}, elapsed, complete, mode}`, plus `changed` when you pass `since` — `results` is keyed by ws_id (not top-level), `complete` means the mode condition held when the wait returned. `starting` means a message you dispatched (spawn_workstream or spawn_batch's `initial_message`, or send_to_workstream to an idle child) hasn't started on the child yet. It isn't terminal, so keep waiting rather than resending. The calls in a response with a wait run one at a time in order, so a send_to_workstream listed before the wait has been dispatched when the wait starts. `stalled` means that message still hasn't started `dispatch_age_s` seconds after you dispatched it; both states carry `dispatch_age_s`, and a child entering either isn't a `since` change. The first wait that sees a child stalled returns early with `complete: false` and lists it in a top-level `stalled`; later waits keep waiting on it. Inspect a stalled child before resending: if your message is among its messages, the child has it (it may be compacting a long context), so give it more time, because a resend would deliver it twice. Close it if it's stuck. Ten minutes after the dispatch a child reads its stored state again; an `idle` child whose `message` doesn't answer yours never ran it. `message` is the child's last assistant text for `idle`/`error`, a short sentinel for `closed`/`not_found`, and `null` for non-terminal rows (and for every row when the wait times out or is interrupted, so read `state` to see which children still need work) and for a finished child whose message couldn't be read (call inspect_workstream for it); capped at 10 KiB UTF-8, with `truncated=true` when the cap fires (call inspect_workstream for the rest). A wait that times out returns states only: the wait that completes carries the finished children's messages, and inspect_workstream reads one now. A child that closed before the completing wait shows only the `closed` sentinel there; inspect_workstream still reads what it produced. Real terminal states: `idle`, `error`, `closed`, `deleted` (the last is unobservable since hard-delete cascades the row out of storage). `mode='any'` returns when the first child hits a real terminal; `mode='all'` returns once every id is real-terminal. Ids are validated up front — ws_ids are exactly 32 hex chars, copy them VERBATIM from spawn_batch/list_workstreams results; a malformed id (truncated/garbled/non-hex) errors immediately with `did_you_mean` suggestions and a roster of your children, and an id that can't be observed (foreign / nonexistent / hard-deleted mid-wait) aborts the wait on the tick that sees it with `state='not_found'` plus top-level `error`/`not_found` fields and, when it can be read, the `children` roster. When that happens, fix the id and re-issue — do NOT assume the child is dead; check `did_you_mean` or re-list. Child display names are labels, not addresses; always target ids. Capped at 32 ws_ids and 600s; both overflows error rather than silently truncating. If the user sends you a message while you wait, the wait returns at once with `interrupted: "user_message"`, `complete: false` and states only, as on a timeout. The user's message normally follows this result (if none does, the user withdrew it): handle it, then call wait_for_workstream again with the same ws_ids if you still need to wait.

ws_ids.description: Workstream ids to wait on (each exactly 32 hex chars, copied verbatim from spawn_batch / list_workstreams results). Accepts 1 or more; capped at 32 per call. Malformed ids fail the call before any waiting; well-formed ids that can't be observed abort it on the first tick — both return did-you-mean suggestions.

timeout.description: Maximum seconds to block. Default 60. Capped at 600 — for longer waits, call again with the same ws_ids.

mode.description: 'any' (default) returns when the first child reaches a real terminal state (idle / error / closed / deleted); 'all' returns once every named child is real-terminal. An id that can't be observed (foreign / nonexistent / deleted mid-wait) aborts the wait immediately with state='not_found' and a top-level error, regardless of mode.

since.description: Optional prior snapshot (typically the `results` dict from an earlier wait_for_workstream call). Besides the `mode` condition, the wait also returns as soon as any child listed in `since` differs from its snapshot (state/tokens/updated); `changed` lists those children (`[]` when the wait returned for another reason). `complete` stays false unless the mode condition holds, so a child that only moved on (e.g. idle to thinking) is not done: read its `state`. When a change alone ends the wait, only the changed children that reached a real terminal state carry their `message`; every other row's is null, as on a timeout. An unchanged child that is already real-terminal still satisfies the mode condition, so `mode='any'` returns at once for it. ws_ids absent from `since` never trigger the early return — they count toward `mode` only, so a disjoint `since` dict doesn't exit on tick one. Omit for the default terminal-state behaviour.
